title: SYSK Selects: How Ponzi Schemes Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the early episode on how Ponzi schemes work. The hosts open with a tangent about an architect duo (Arakawa and Madeline Gins) and their 'immortality' architecture, then tie in investors hurt by Bernard Madoff. They trace Charles Ponzi's 1920s postal reply coupon scheme (the company's returns were promised too fast, and the scheme was exposed when the number of coupons in circulation didn't add up), explain the mechanics of paying early investors with later investors' money, and compare Ponzi schemes with pyramid schemes (Amway and Pampered Chef are cited as legitimate pyramid-model businesses). Earlier examples include Sarah Howe's Boston scheme in the 1880s and William Franklin Miller. They cover Lou Pearlman, who funded the Backstreet Boys and 'N Sync, and the 2006 collapse of a Albanian Ponzi scheme that caused unrest. They discuss Bernard Madoff's affinity fraud, his steady 11% returns, the SEC's failure to act on complaints, and his later confession. Warning signs and advice on protecting yourself follow. The episode ends with plugs for the Stuff You Should Know spoken word album and the blog, and listener mail correcting the 'theory' vs. 'hypothesis' usage, the Burma/Myanmar note, and the term 'yoni'.

segments.title: Opening banter and Selects introduction
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this Saturday Selects rerun of the Ponzi schemes episode, and the hosts riff on an architecture duo's undulating-floor buildings and Bernard Madoff's reach.

segments.title: Charles Ponzi and the reply coupon scheme
segments.summary: The hosts explain Charles Ponzi's 1920s scheme, which exploited international reply coupons bought cheaply abroad and sold in the US, and how it unraveled when the coupon count did not match the claimed volume.

segments.title: How Ponzi schemes work
segments.summary: The mechanics: early investors are paid with later investors' money, which attracts more investors until the scheme inevitably collapses. The hosts compare it to a pyramid scheme and note that Ponzi schemes involve no real investment.

segments.title: Early Ponzi schemes: Sarah Howe and William Franklin Miller
segments.summary: Earlier schemes from the 1880s and around 1900 include Sarah Howe's Boston women's Liberty bond scheme and William Franklin Miller's scheme, both predating Charles Ponzi.

segments.title: Lou Pearlman and the boy bands
segments.summary: Lou Pearlman, who funded the Backstreet Boys and 'N Sync, was exposed in 2006 as running a Ponzi scheme for about twenty years. His sentence and repayments are described.

segments.title: Albania's Ponzi scheme collapse
segments.summary: A group of Ponzi schemers in Albania took about two billion dollars, roughly a third of the country's GDP, and the collapse led to unrest, with riots and deaths.

segments.title: Bernard Madoff and affinity fraud
segments.summary: Bernard Madoff used affinity fraud through an exclusive Jewish country club in Florida, offered believable steady returns of about eleven percent, and ran a legitimate business alongside. Barron's warned in 2001 and the SEC failed to act on complaints. He is said to have stolen about fifty billion dollars.

segments.title: Warning signs and how to protect yourself
segments.summary: The hosts cover red flags such as too-good-to-be-true returns, high-pressure pitches, and too-steady growth. They advise asking questions, knowing where money is invested, and diversifying so a scam cannot bankrupt you, and note that reporting to the SEC is an option.

segments.title: Madoff's confession and personal security
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Madoff's confession, doubts that he acted alone, and the reported security spending on his Manhattan penthouse after he was caught.

segments.title: Spoken word album and blog plugs
segments.summary: Promotion for the Stuff You Should Know spoken word economics album and the hosts' blog.

segments.title: Listener mail: theory vs hypothesis, Burma, yoni
segments.summary: Listener corrections: Sarah notes that 'theory' and 'hypothesis' are used incorrectly, the Burma/Myanmar name is clarified, and Stephanie notes the Sanskrit term 'yoni' for the female genitalia.
